newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Euro-MPs to approve comparative advertising directive.
newsitem.headline: Euro-MPs to approve comparative advertising directive.

text.p: Advertisements which directly compare named products, such as French Bordeaux wine and Italian Chianti, may become a more frequent sight in Europe if Euro-MPs approve the idea, as expected, on October 22.
"I think this is a good idea. Why shouldn't there be comparative advertising?" rapporteur Ria Oomen-Ruijten, a Dutch Christian Democrat, told Reuters on Wednesday.

The idea was first proposed in May 1991, when the European Commission said a 1984 directive, 84/450/EEC, outlawing misleading advertising should be amended to make direct comparisions possible in adverts in all member states.

The Council accepted the idea in its common position in March, on the grounds that adverts helped create outlets for goods throughout the EU internal market and that the current situation, in which some countries allowed comparative advertising but others banned it, harmed consumers, sponsors and advertisers and distorted competition.
The European Parliament is expected to adopt the draft directive, COM(91)147, at the October plenary session, but only once a number of significant changes have been made.

Oomen-Ruijten, reporting for the parliament's committee on consumer protection, will recommend reducing the limitations the Council has imposed on comparative advertising, sometimes known as "knocking copy".
The rapporteur accepts the Council's view that advertisers should only compare goods which meet the same needs and focus objectively on their specific features.

But she rejects ministers' idea that advertisers should be prevented from comparing their goods with products which have an exclusive trade mark, like McDonald's hamburgers, or a regional name, for example camembert cheese.

"This would protect huge trade marks and products with designation of origin from competition. (Our amendment) makes it possible for small companies and new marks to make themselves known," an assistant for Oomen-Ruijten said.

The committee cited a case in which McDonald's told the owner of the McMunchies sandwich shop in England last month to take down her sign or face legal action. The hamburger giant said it was the registered user of the prefix "Mc".
A majority of Euro-MPs are likely to support Oomen-Ruijten's position, although she expects opposition from French colleagues.
The rapporteur also thinks an advertiser should be allowed to cite the results of tests comparing his product with other named brands, even if it was responsible for carrying out the tests.
She disagreed this would lead to abuse, even if the advertising industry were allowed to self-regulate, as she proposes.

Misleading advertising was, and would remain, forbidden, she said, adding: "Self-regulation is simple, cost-effective and always works. If it doesn't work, then you can make a legal complaint afterwards."
